orderHint: Click the parts in order · click one again to take it back
actSpeakBrief: One of you is the examiner and holds the clock. Swap after each task.
actSpeak1: Ask six Part 1 questions about food, weekends and where your partner lives. Every answer must have a second move. Stop them the moment one does not.
actSpeak2: Give them the card describe a person who taught you something. One minute of notes, then talk. Cut them off at exactly two minutes and say where they were.
actSpeak3: Run it again, but this time interrupt twice with a question. The task is to answer and get back to the talk without losing the thread.
actWriteBrief: Write the one minute of notes for that card — words, not sentences — and then the full two-minute talk. Two hundred and fifty words is roughly two minutes. Write it out once so you know how much language that actually is.
coverSub: Speaking Parts 1 and 2 — how long an answer should be, how to extend one without waffling, and how to fill the two minutes of the long turn.
s1Title: Eleven to fourteen minutes, three parts
s1ColA: Part 1 — about twelve questions on three everyday topics. Part 2 — a card, one minute to prepare, then you talk. Part 3 — a discussion of the same topic, but abstract.
s1ColB: One test for Academic and General Training, marked identically. Four criteria, 25% each: Fluency & Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammar, Pronunciation. All four are about language.
s1Note: Nothing here is marked on what you know. The examiner does not care whether your opinion is right, or whether the story is true. The topic is only an excuse to produce English.
s2ColA: Every Part 1 answer is two moves: answer the question, then give one reason, example or contrast. Two or three sentences. That is the whole shape.
s2ColB: One word leaves the examiner nothing to mark. A speech is no better — the examiner has about twelve questions to fit into five minutes, so you will be cut off, and the rest of what you planned is never heard.
s2Note: Part 1 is the easy part and candidates still lose marks in it, almost always by answering as though it were a conversation with a stranger rather than a language test.
s3Title: One minute to prepare, two to talk
s3ColA: The card has a task and three or four bullets. They are a spine, not a checklist — you are not marked on ticking them off, and the last one is usually worth the most time.
s3ColB: Aim for the full two minutes. That is roughly 250 words at a natural pace — far more language than most candidates expect, which is why so many stop at forty seconds.
s3Note: Use the minute for notes, not sentences. Anything you write as a full sentence you will read aloud, and read-aloud English sounds nothing like spoken English.
s4Title: Which answer is the right shape?
s5Title: What does a one-word answer cost?
s6ColA: Give a reason. …because I never learnt properly.
s6ColB: Give an example. …last week I made the same thing four times.
s6ColC: Compare with the past. …I used to cook a lot more before I moved.
s6ColD: Qualify it. …though it depends how much time I have.
s6Note: The past comparison is the most useful of the four: it forces a second tense into an answer that would otherwise sit entirely in the present.

s9Title: Two words that buy you a clause
s9Ctx: Both of these rescue an answer that came out too short.
s10Title: Opening and closing the long turn
s10Ctx: Two sentences that make a two-minute talk sound organised rather than improvised.

s14Title: You hear yourself make a mistake
x06a: Polite and empty. It answers the question and then stops, so there is nothing to assess beyond one verb.
x06b: This answers a different question — what people should do. Part 1 asks about you, and an abstract answer here reads as avoidance.
x06c: Answer, then a reason and a consequence. Two moves, about fifteen words, and every word of it is about you.
x06d: Length without content. Five short clauses that all say the same thing show less range than one sentence with a reason in it.
x07a: Fluency is judged on sustaining speech. One word is accurate and unmarkable — there is no sample of language in it at all.
x07b: Comprehension is not one of the four criteria. The examiner can hear that it was understood; there is simply nothing else to hear.
x07c: Grammar marks what you produce, so a short answer starves that criterion too — but the criterion this most obviously damages is Fluency and Coherence.
x07d: There is no rule about sentence counts anywhere in the band descriptors. Two or three sentences is a habit that works, not a requirement.
x09a: Specific, personal, and it puts a past tense in without being asked. This is what an unrehearsed answer sounds like.
x09b: Honest and slightly unexpected, which is a good sign. Refusing the premise of a question is perfectly acceptable if you say what you do instead.
x09c: Short but complete: a preference, an admission that it is unexamined, and a reason. Not memorised — nobody rehearses a shrug.
x09d: Register far above the question, and it never answers it. Examiners hear this daily and it reads as recitation — which is marked down, because it is not spontaneous speech.
x10a: Stopping early is exactly what the two-minute target exists to prevent. The examiner will not fill the silence for you.
x10b: Depth beats coverage. One bullet reopened with a concrete example is worth more than four bullets ticked off, and it is the move that reliably fills the time.
x10c: A new topic is off-task, and off-task speech costs marks under Coherence however fluent it is.
x10d: Repeating the card's own words adds no language of yours. The examiner is marking what you produce, not what was printed.
x11a: Though — one word, and it obliges you to produce a second clause in a second tense. The cheapest extension in the language.
x11b: Depends buys thinking time without being a filler, and it sets up a condition — which is a grammar structure the examiner can mark.
x12a: Talk about — name the subject in the first sentence, then get to the detail. It costs four seconds and tells the examiner you have a plan.
x12b: Before I finish adds fifteen seconds and signals that you are ending deliberately rather than running out — the difference the examiner actually hears.
x13a: The last bullet is almost always the why, and it is almost always the one candidates rush. It is the only part of the card that asks for a judgement rather than a fact, so it is where the better language lives.
x14a: Examiners do interrupt, but to manage the clock rather than to re-ask. Being redirected is not itself the penalty.
x14b: Close, and the reason many candidates believe it: knowledge genuinely is not marked. Relevance still is, and that is a different thing.
x14c: Task Response is a Writing criterion. It does not exist in the Speaking test, so nothing here is scored under that name.
x14d: There is no content criterion in Speaking — but Coherence covers whether the response fits the question, so relevance is marked even though knowledge is not.
x15a: Name the subject, place them, then say what the talk will cover. Ten seconds spent here makes the next hundred sound organised — and it gives you somewhere to return to if you dry up.
x16a: Self-correction is explicitly normal in spoken English and is not penalised. Leaving an error you noticed helps nobody.
x16b: One clean correction shows control and costs almost nothing. It is repeated restarting that damages Fluency, not the act of correcting itself.
x16c: Restarting whole sentences is the habit that actually costs Fluency marks, because it breaks the flow far more than the original error did.
x16d: Apologising spends time on something that is not being marked, and it draws attention to an error the examiner may have already discounted.
